definition: The first day of August (Old Style), observed in medieval England as a harvest festival at which loaves baked from the first-cut wheat were offered in church; now a quarter-day in the Scottish legal calendar, falling on 28 August.
etymology: From Old English hlāfmæsse, a compound of hlāf meaning loaf and mæsse meaning mass or feast. The loaf in question was not bread for eating but a ritual first-fruit, carried to the altar as a tithe of the harvest. Over centuries the aspirate softened and the word collapsed into lammas, losing the memory of its wheat entirely.
usage: August 15 sits squarely in what older almanacs called Lammas-tide, the loose fortnight around the feast when grain stood ready to fall. A farmer watching thunderheads build over a ripening field might still mutter that lammas weather is never to be trusted — brilliant one hour, ruinous the next.
